title: Iwuk Edesi
localName: Iwuk edesi — native jollof, palm oil rice
author: Iquo Bassey
desc: Native jollof — two cups of rice cooked in a litre of palm-oil stock with smoked shrimp and dried fish, and a bunch of chopped ugwu stirred through for the last five minutes.
longDesc: Iwuk edesi is palm oil rice, and the author describes it as the way our grandmothers cooked one-pot rice dishes back in the day. It has nothing in common with party jollof except that it is rice in a sauce: no tomato paste, no curry powder, no foil lid. A cooking spoon of palm oil, ground tomatoes and pepper, half a cup of smoked shrimp, a cup of dried fish and the beef stock make the cooking liquid, the washed rice goes in to absorb it, and a medium bunch of chopped ikong or ugwu goes through at the end.
ingredients: 1 medium bunch ikong or ugwu, chopped
2 cooking spoons tomatoes and pepper, ground
// Used in the method but not listed in the original
1 onion, half for the beef and half for frying
steps: Season and boil the beef with the beef seasoning, half an onion, salt and the half teaspoon of dried pepper. Keep the stock.
Wash the rice and set it aside.
Heat the palm oil and fry the remaining onion.
Add the ground tomatoes and pepper, the shrimps, the dried fish, the beef, the ground crayfish, the remaining seasoning and salt to taste.
Pour in the water and the available meat stock, and boil 10 minutes.
Add the washed rice and cook until it is almost soft and dry.
Add the chopped vegetable and cook about 5 minutes.
chefTips: Almost soft and dry is the cue for the rice, and the 'almost' matters — it finishes in the five minutes with the greens.
A litre of water plus the beef stock to two cups of rice. That is generous, because the dried fish and shrimp absorb a good deal.
One cooking spoon of palm oil only. This is not a heavy dish despite being called palm oil rice — the oil is for flavour and colour.
Fry the onion in the palm oil before anything else. It is the base of the whole sauce.
Ugwu or ikong goes in at the very end, chopped. Five minutes and no more.
No tomato paste, no curry powder, no thyme. Those belong to party jollof (NGA109) and would make this a different dish entirely.
Onion is used twice in the method and appears nowhere in the ingredient list. One bulb, split in half, is what the method implies.
commonMistakes: Cooking the rice fully before the greens go in.
Using more palm oil, which makes it greasy rather than flavoured.
Overcooking the ugwu to a grey mush.
sources: Adapted from 'How to make Iwuk Edesi – Native Jollof Rice', published by 1Q Food Platter. BYLINE: none appears on the page; credited to the site. Quantities as printed: 2 cups rice; 1 medium bunch Ikong or Ugwu (chopped); 6 pieces of Beef; 1/2 cup smoked Shrimp; 1 cup dried Fish; 2 cooking spoons Tomatoes/Pepper (ground); 1/2 teaspoon dried Pepper; A cooking spoon Palm oil; 1 tbsp ground Crayfish; One crayfish seasoning tablet; 1 beef seasoning cube; A litre Water; salt to taste. Yield not specified.

LIST/METHOD MISMATCH, flagged: onion is used TWICE in the method — '1/2 onion' with the beef and 'fry the remaining onion' — but is ABSENT from the ingredient list entirely. Listed above under a clear heading.

Method and cues as printed: season and boil the meat with beef seasoning, 1/2 onion, salt and 1/2 tsp dry pepper; wash the rice; heat the oil and fry the remaining onion; add the ground tomatoes and pepper, shrimps, fish, beef, ground crayfish, remaining seasoning and salt; 'pour the water and available meat stock and boil for 10 minutes'; add the washed rice and cook 'until almost soft and dry'; 'finally add the chopped vegetable and cook for about 5 minutes'.
Headnote as printed: 'Iwuk Edesi or palm oil rice is the way our grandmothers cooked one pot rice dishes back in the day' — Efik origin, framed as a nostalgic household dinner.
A SECOND SOURCE EXISTS and was not retrieved: Sisi Jemimah's 'Native Jollof Rice (Iwuk Edesi)'. Noted as a lead rather than used.

ON ITS DOCUMENTATION STATUS: a prior research pass listed iwuk edesi among dishes 'simply absent from the named-author record'. It is documented with full quantities, on a site that pass under-searched.
reheating: Steam or microwave with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Red palm oil supplies carotenoids and vitamin E.
Ugwu adds iron, calcium and fibre to a rice dish.
Smoked shrimp and dried fish give lean protein, iodine and calcium.
culturalNote: Native jollof is the honest name for this: rice cooked in palm oil with whatever smoked and dried seafood the household had, which is what rice dishes looked like before tomato paste and curry powder arrived. It is called iwuk edesi among the Efik, and versions of the same idea — concoction rice, palm oil rice — turn up across southern Nigeria under local names.
